props.title: The Paleface

sections.content: Buster Keaton's The Paleface (1922) stands as a brilliant early example of combining social commentary with slapstick comedy. The film subverts typical Western tropes by positioning Keaton's character alongside Native Americans fighting against greedy oil barons. This was revolutionary for its time, predating more socially conscious Westerns like Broken Arrow (1950) by decades. Keaton's physical comedy reaches spectacular heights, particularly in the famous chase sequences and the scene where he dons traditional Native American garments.

sections.content: The film's technical achievements deserve special attention. Shot by Elgin Lessley, who worked on many of Keaton's best films including The Navigator (1924), The Paleface demonstrates sophisticated camera work unusual for early 1920s comedy. The chase sequences through the forest and cliff-side stunts required precise timing and innovative cinematography techniques that influenced physical comedy for generations.

Keaton's approach to Native American representation, while still reflecting 1920s limitations, was notably more sympathetic than contemporary films like The Indian Land Grab (1920) or The Battle at Elderbush Gulch (1913). His character sides with the tribe against corrupt businessmen, offering an early critique of exploitation themes that wouldn't become common in Westerns until the 1950s with films like Broken Arrow (1950) and Devil's Doorway (1950). sections.content: The film's stunt work remains impressive even by modern standards. Keaton's famous fall from the cliff, while wearing full Native American ceremonial dress, exemplifies his commitment to dangerous physical comedy that influenced later comedians from Jackie Chan to Johnny Knoxville. This dedication to practical effects connects directly to later silent masterpieces like Safety Last! (1923) and modern practical stunt work in films like Mission: Impossible - Fallout (2018).
